sections.title: The brief
sections.body:
CloudChipr is a cloud-cost observability, management, and automation platform for engineering and finance teams.

My role was to turn complex cloud operations into an understandable MVP: teams could schedule workflows, send Slack alerts, create Jira tickets, and deactivate unused resources across AWS, GCP, and Azure.

sections.title: Concept Selection

sections.title: How it started
sections.body:
Imagine being a UX designer exploring the world of cloud systems like AWS, GCP, and Azure. Sounds hard ha?

I joined a team of expert SRE and DevOps engineers when the project was just starting, moving from being a solo designer. Back then, all I had were a concept and a few rough mockups. As I was relatively new to this field, I decided to start with the basics – fundamental learning. This study covered a series of important steps that I needed to work through.

sections.body: I enrolled in a course on Udemy (218 lectures in total). Think of it as a crash course in cloud language and landscape. It helped me understand the jargon and navigate the territory better.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.body:
I have seen 1000s of 💸 per Hour of cloud waste paid for years just because:

Companies waste a large percentage of their cloud cost to pay for resources that are never used.
Developers forget to cleanup after tests.
Automation tools fail in the middle of execution and leave the cloud resources.
Finances and business do not have context whether the growing cloud cost is a waste.

Based on the personal research and information gathered from interviewing company’s founders and key stakeholders there is a clear need for a strong cost optimization platform that can effectively address the issue of wasting thousands of dollars per hour.

sections.title: Problem Discovered During User Research
sections.body: Every day, SRE and DevOps teams face a common issue - the considerable effort they put into cost optimization. This involves a lot of work to make sure things are efficient and cost-effective in the cloud. However, there's also the challenge of human errors that comes into play. Sometimes, mistakes happen, like setting things up wrong or not managing resources properly. These errors can undo the hard work of cost optimization, making the job more complicated for SRE and DevOps teams.

sections.title: Competitor Analysis
sections.body:
When looking at other companies in the field, I did two kinds of analysis: direct and indirect competitors. For direct competitors, I checked out companies with similar products or services as mine. I looked at what they offer, how much they charge, and who they target. This helped me see how I compare in terms of strengths and weaknesses.

Indirect competitors were a bit different. These are companies that might not do exactly what I do, but they could still take customers away. I researched them to understand their potential impact on my market.

I did a lot of research, reading reports, and checking what customers say online. This gave me a good sense of what people like and don't like about my competitors. And I didn't just stop at that. I also looked into the technology they use and any unique things they offer. In the end, all this info helped me figure out where I stand compared to others and how I can stand out.

sections.title: To Design or Not to Design system?
sections.body:
The company has tasked me with determining whether to purchase license of on of the existing design systems or to create a new one. Beyond the pros and cons that contribute to this decision, there's an effective approach I've undertaken – calculating the Return on Investment (ROI) for developing my own design system. This analytical method provides a clear and strategic means of comprehending the optimal direction to take.

Total ROI for One Project
ROI = Cost Savings - Cost of Design System Implementation
$8000 - $20,000 = -$12,000

The decision was clear-cut. After thorough research among various available solutions, I concluded that MUI was the ideal choice.

sections.title: About project
sections.body: Material Exchange is a digital platform that facilitates the efficient and streamlined exchange of material information between brands, manufacturers, and suppliers in the fashion and footwear industry.

sections.caption: Initial wireframes of single material page.

sections.title: Discovery Phase
sections.body:
Imagine Nike's material manager journeying to Vietnam, seeking sustainable materials to be used as a small peace for Air Jordans. Collaborating with local suppliers, they usually assess quality, recycling, and sustainability, incurring costs of $15,000 for travel and $10,000 for testing. This risk underscores Nike's commitment to responsible sourcing (only 15% of positive findings).

Companies like Nike spend millions on such research, but just a fraction proves valuable. So, material digitalization is needed for cost savings. The potential to revolutionize sourcing and sustainability drives ongoing innovation.

sections.caption: A tour of the Goodwill Outlet warehouse and retail store in St. Paul, MN, in April 2019.

sections.body:
Fashion is responsible for 10 percent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions and 20 percent of global wastewater, and uses more energy than the aviation and shipping sectors combined. Global fashion also consumes 93 billion metric tons of clean water each year, about half of what Americans drink annually.

Since the 2000s, fashion production has doubled and it will likely triple by 2050, according to the American Chemical Society. Ninety-two million tonnes of unwanted fabrics are disposed of each year, and 14.5 million tons of textiles were landfilled and incinerated in 2018.

Leftover fabrics have already been produced, so there is no expenditure of water, energy, or virgin raw materials to create something new. With Material Exchange, they are available and accessible on a global level for brands to use in upcoming collections.

sections.caption: Screenshot of “Deadstock Depot”. Online services allows to sell purchase deadstock fabrics.

sections.title: User Research
sections.body: To ensure a user-centered approach to my decisions, I conducted a comprehensive survey to validate my assumptions about Material Exchange. With an impressive participation of 160 individuals from 24 different countries, I gained valuable insights into the needs and preferences of my user base. Analyzing the survey data allowed me to confirm my assumptions, identify common trends, and prioritize improvements based on user feedback.

I made it a practice to conduct iterative user interview and testing sessions at least twice a month. This involved engaging both new users and maintaining connections with existing ones. At first, I experimented with recruiting users through the usertesting.com platform. However, I soon realized that custom user recruitment is significantly more effective. Platform users often exhibit strong biases that can impact the quality of my insights.

Combining insights from various sources—company strategy, user research, quantitative surveys, and competitive analyses—I crafted my initial hypothetical personas. This marked the beginning of my ongoing process to discover new user archetypes throughout the journey.

sections.title: HMW Statements

columns.body:
• How might I effectively centralize and organize digital materials and assets, providing easy searchability and accessibility for brands, manufacturers, and suppliers within the Material Exchange platform?
  • How might I enhance collaboration and communication between teams by integrating feedback and approval processes seamlessly within the Material Exchange platform, ensuring efficient collaboration and minimizing miscommunication?
  • How might I assist brands in maintaining consistent and cohesive material usage across different teams and stakeholders, leveraging the Material Exchange platform’s capabilities?

• How might I automate manual tasks and streamline workflows within the Material Exchange platform to significantly improve efficiency, saving valuable time for all users involved?
  • How might I ensure robust access controls and permissions within the Material Exchange platform, prioritizing data security and confidentiality to protect sensitive information?
  • How might I provide valuable analytics and insights on material usage and performance within the Material Exchange platform, empowering data-driven decision-making for brands, manufacturers, and suppliers?
  • How might I guarantee seamless scalability and integration of the Material Exchange platform with other tools and systems used by brands, manufacturers, and suppliers, ensuring smooth operations and compatibility?

sections.title: Personalized Approach

columns.title: Personalized Dashboard
columns.body: Centralized interface that offers users an instant overview of their material assets. It provides real-time insights into the status, location, and usage of materials, streamlining inventory management and enhancing decision-making.

columns.title: Smart Search
columns.body: Smart Search empowers users to quickly and intelligently locate specific materials within their inventory. Using advanced search algorithms and filters, it understands user queries and offers real-time suggestions as users type, making the search process highly efficient.

sections.title: User testing & findings
Material managers struggle, spending too much time adding materials to folders.
sections.body:
🕒 Exp. Duration — 45 min
❌ Act. Result — 61 min

In a usability test, a material manager was asked to create a winter-fall collection of materials. This involved making folders for different categories and then finding and adding materials to those folders.

Interestingly, a lot of time was spent opening and closing folders repeatedly. The manager also had to add each material individually, which took up a large portion of the session.

Surprisingly, about 60% of the total time was used just for managing folders and adding materials. This left only 40% for more important work such as decision-making and evaluating materials.

As a solution, I introduced an innovative feature named “Dropzone”. Drawing inspiration from people's familiarity with operating system folders, Dropzone enables users to effortlessly drag and drop files, mirroring a natural experience.

To enhance efficiency, I added the capability to select multiple items and utilize multiple dropzones, streamlining the process of managing up to 4 folders within a single task. This approach not only simplifies the user experience but also significantly accelerates the material management process.

🕒 Exp. Duration — 45 min
🎉 Act. Result — 23 min
Users frequently conduct similar searches, resulting in repetitive manual entry of search criteria and potential frustration due to redundancy.

Easier grouping of search criteria would simplify repetitive operations by enabling users to execute the same search with a single click. To address this need, I introduced and tested the “Save Search” feature.

sections.title: Why Are Some Materials Overlooked by Brands? The Influence of Image Editing Knowledge and Budget Constraints
sections.body:
During my regular observations and interviews with users from various backgrounds, I noticed a consistent pattern: Brands paid more attention to materials that looked good with attractive images and well-designed cards. This phenomenon is known as the Aesthetic Usability Effect, where people tend to judge content based on its appearance.

And here's the catch: Because of this phenomenon, brands didn't seem to pay as much attention to materials that didn't meet their visual standards. To understand why, I dug deeper.

After engaging in discussions with users, I understood the root cause of this unexpected behavior. It became obvious that many suppliers, especially smaller ones and individuals, faced significant challenges due to their limited image editing skills and budget constraints. These constraints prevented them from effectively utilizing quality image editing tools.

It's important to note that image editing softwares like Photoshop are quite complex for basic operations, such are crop or resize an image, and many material managers either aren't familiar with it or lack access due to licensing limitations.

sections.title: the Problem
Objective
sections.body: My objective is to enhance the Material Exchange Marketplace's image presentation capabilities by providing easy and intuitive design tool for material managers.

sections.title: Anticipated Transformations: The Impact of My Image Editing Tool on Material Exchange
sections.body:
• With the implementation of my tool, I anticipate a substantial increase in material engagement. I predict that materials edited using my platform will experience a 30% boost in engagement, piquing the interest of brands and users alike.
  • My analysis suggests that materials with professionally edited images and well-designed cards will exhibit a 20% improvement in conversion rates compared to non-enhanced materials.
  • With the tool now available, I anticipate attracting and onboarding a larger number of small suppliers and individuals. My projections indicate a 40% growth in my supplier base within the first year of tool implementation.
  • I predict a significant enhancement in user satisfaction as a direct result of this tool. I anticipate that 90% of my users will report an improved experience, noting that the tool makes it easier for them to create visually appealing materials.
  • Brands are expected to demonstrate heightened interest in materials from a more diverse set of suppliers, including smaller businesses and individuals. My projections indicate a 25% increase in brand interactions with these suppliers.

sections.title: About the project

Hotel Apartments is a flexible online booking service specializing in extended-stay hotel room bookings. Easily browse and book carefully selected serviced apartments and villas, providing you with spacious, budget-friendly, and all-inclusive lodging options.

The business became profitable in its first year and surpassed $5M in revenue. The product connected that unusual market demand with a clearer booking experience.

sections.title: According to official statistics, the number of Russian citizens living in Dubai increased by 170% between February and June 2022.
sections.body:
Since the start of the Russian-Ukrainian War in February 2022, there has been a significant increase in the number of Russians moving to Dubai.

A number of companies have opened offices in Dubai and financed their employees’ relocation along with their families including:

  • Visa
  • Alphabet Inc's Google
  • Talnet, a company matching tech workers from Eastern Europe with startups worldwide

Hotel apartments offer them a flexible, convenient, and comfortable living arrangement as they navigate the challenges of relocation. With fully furnished spaces, on-site amenities, and services tailored to their needs, hotel apartments not only ease the transition but also foster a sense of community and support in a new and unfamiliar environment.

sections.title: Field Studies
sections.body:
Since the hotel industry was new to me, I began with a field study. I embarked on a business trip where my client had invited me to their had office in Dubai. The objective was to immerse myself in the world of hotel apartment rental services, understand the competitive landscape, and conduct user research to document the primary pain points and challenges faced by potential and existing customers.

Upon arriving at the airport in Dubai, I was greeted by Shabahir Ibn Muhammad, the Guest Relations Officer (GRO): one of the key stakeholders in this business. During my one-hour trip to my apartment, I started interviewing him because I knew he had important insights. I talked about the challenges guests faced, their preferences, and how the company helped them. This was my first step in understanding the hotel apartment rental industry in Dubai.

sections.title: Walking a Mile in the User's Shoes
sections.body: As the website already existed, one of my main goals was to understand the current customer experience and identify the issues that led to drop-offs (87%), as well as why some users chose competitors over my service. In meetings and interviews with users who visited my office in person, I asked them to replicate their actions on my website, offering them gifts that I had brought with me from Yerevan (magnets, candies, etc.).

sections.title: Findings
sections.body:
• Many users found it frustrating that they couldn't book a hotel apartment instantly. Instead, they had to send an inquiry and wait for a response.
  • Users had trouble finding similar properties when they used specific filters that resulted in no search results.
  • People planning long stays cared a lot about knowing facilities around the place they're booking, especially if they have children and need to find schools. They were also concerned about extra costs, like transportation.
  • Users wanted to know exactly how much they'd be paying, including all bills, right from the start.

sections.title: Tempo
sections.subtitle: Safe special delivery for important documents and time-sensitive items.

sections.title: About the project
sections.body:
Tempo is a safe special-delivery service built around documents and other time-sensitive items. It lets a customer request a trusted courier, confirm the sender and the recipient, and follow the delivery from pickup to handoff. The same route model carries food, pharmacy items and custom errands, but the promise at the centre is document safety: the right item, handled by the right courier, delivered to the intended person.

My role. I was the product designer on Tempo from the first conversation with the founder, Chant Khialian, to the handover of the UI kit — experience strategy, information architecture, core flows, interface design and the component library — with Anna Avalyan joining me on the visual system in the last phase. One founder, one developer, one designer, and a business that needed to take orders before it had an app.

The constraint that shaped everything. Couriers were already delivering by phone. Whatever I designed had to be understood by customers who had never used a multi-stop product, and by couriers who had never used the app at all.

sections.title: Orders were taken before the app existed, the route became the product, and one assumption is still waiting for its test
sections.body:
The multi-stop route model reached a state the team could build and the founder could sell. Discovery, order building, route review, checkout and tracking exist as one connected flow, and the component library behind them was handed to the developer so a new category can be added without redesigning the order.

I am proud of the honest part too. The route sheet has not yet been tested with paying customers adding a third stop in a live session. That behaviour is the assumption the product rests on, and I would rather say so than let a polished screen suggest otherwise.

items.label: weeks between the landing page going live and the first app build - the service ran on a phone number in between
stops in one order at launch, up from one: the number the whole interface is designed around
hallway tests of the route sheet, four of which failed before the plus button moved to where it is now

sections.title: Several errands often happen at the same time
sections.body:
A customer orders dinner while an important document waits across town. Every delivery app I looked at treats those as two orders: another checkout, another courier, another fee, another tracking screen to keep open.

Tempo needed one flow that could combine different requests without making the trip feel complicated. A customer had to understand where the courier would go, what another stop did to the price and the time, and when the whole order would arrive. If any of those three was unclear, the customer would simply place two orders — and Tempo would be an ordinary delivery app with a nicer logo.

sections.title: One order, several stops, one courier
sections.body:
Customers add food, documents, pharmacy items or a custom address to the same delivery. Tempo groups those stops, proposes an efficient order and keeps the route visible before checkout.

The product explains the benefit at the moment it matters. A time-saved message appears on the map, and the route sheet lists each stop and lets the customer adjust the plan before the courier starts. The rule I kept coming back to: never make someone leave the order to change the route.

sections.title: Four phases, and the third one is where it nearly went wrong

items.label: Study delivery apps and route planners
items.text: I ordered from every local delivery app I could find and planned routes in tools built for drivers. Two mental models, no product that held both.

items.label: Map categories, orders and multi-stop journeys
items.text: One diagram of how an order grows from one address to three. It stayed on the wall for the whole project and was wrong twice.

items.label: Test the route model in wireframes
items.text: The first wireframes hid the route behind a tab. In hallway tests nobody found it. Moving the plus button into the order itself was the single most important decision on the project.

items.label: Build the UI and the component library
items.text: Screens, states and a kit the developer could extend. The last week was spent making sure a new category could be added without me.

sections.title: Four goals, and the route had to serve all of them

items.label: Let customers manage different delivery needs in one app
items.text: Food, documents and a pharmacy run should feel like one errand, not three apps.

items.label: Show each stop, route change and arrival expectation
items.text: No surprises at checkout: the price and the time move on screen when a stop is added.

items.label: Make another pickup feel like part of the current order
items.text: The plus button lives inside the order. Adding a stop should feel like adding an item.

items.label: Give the team reusable patterns for new categories
items.text: A category is a data change, not a redesign. The kit had to prove that before I left.

sections.title: Delivery apps taught me conventions. Route planners taught me sequence.
sections.body:
I reviewed the local delivery products to learn the patterns customers already trust for browsing, checkout and tracking, and I studied route-planning tools because Tempo’s core interaction depends on ordering several locations.

The comparison exposed the gap. Delivery apps handled products well but treated every order as a closed journey. Route planners handled stops well but had no shopping context. Tempo needed both mental models in one interface — and, as I found out a phase later, needed them in the same screen, not in neighbouring tabs.

sections.title: The plus button turns one delivery into a route
sections.body:
A customer can add another pickup without leaving the active order. The new address joins the route sheet, and Tempo updates the map and the estimated time.

Contextual guidance introduces the feature at the moment it becomes useful. Customers learn the route model through the task, not through a tutorial — which matters, because the first version of this screen had a tutorial, and nobody read it.

items.caption: Where it started: one address, one delivery
items.text: The first flow asked for a location, took one order and ended on a tracking dot. Clean, familiar, and exactly what every other app did. A customer with a second errand had to start again.

items.caption: Enter through the need you recognise
items.text: Food, pharmacy, documents, a custom pickup — categories and filters open the service from whichever errand the customer has in mind.

items.caption: Build the order in place
items.text: Items stay attached to their stop and the stop stays attached to the route. Summary, payment and delivery details sit on one screen.

items.caption: Press plus: another pickup joins the sheet
items.text: The new address slides into the route sheet with its own time and distance. Nothing is left, nothing is re-entered — the order simply grows. This is the button that was behind a tab in version one.

items.caption: The map re-plans and says what it saved
items.text: Tempo redraws the path, numbers the stops and shows the minutes saved. Customers can drag a stop to reorder and start the delivery without losing the map.

items.caption: Track the route, not a dot
items.text: Tracking follows the whole route: each stop, each hand-off, one arrival estimate, and the courier’s name and rating next to it.

sections.title: Wireframes made the route model testable — and showed me it was hidden
sections.body:
I mapped the path from category discovery to order building, route review, checkout and tracking, and drew it in low fidelity so it could be tested in an afternoon rather than argued about in a week.

The first round failed. I had put the route on its own tab, next to the order, because it felt tidy. Eleven hallway tests later, four people had never opened it and two asked why the price had changed. So the route moved into the order, the plus button moved to where the items are, and the tab disappeared. It was the least glamorous week of the project and the most useful one.

The wireframes also connected the supporting journeys — sign-in, profiles, order history and delivery preferences — so the developer could see the whole product before any of it was pretty.

sections.title: Categories organize a broad service without hiding the route
sections.body:
Tempo covers food, pharmacy items, alcohol, shops, documents and custom deliveries. Categories and filters let customers enter through the need they recognise.

The route stays the shared layer underneath all of them. A customer can move between shopping and delivery planning while the current stops stay intact — the one rule I refused to trade for a simpler screen.

sections.title: A consistent experience across different requests
sections.body:
Restaurant cards, pharmacy listings, document delivery and custom pickups use the same product language. Customers keep familiar controls as the content changes.

Small choices support the wider service: delivery preferences that reduce waste, saved details that speed up repeat orders, and an account history that keeps past routes one tap away. None of it is clever. All of it is the difference between an app people try and an app people keep.

sections.title: The same language from sign-in to tip
sections.body: Account, orders, notifications, route and rating share one set of controls, so a customer who has placed one order can read every other screen.

sections.title: Sensitive deliveries need more than a tracking dot
sections.body:
Document delivery raised the bar on trust. A customer needs to know the courier received the correct item and handed it to the intended person — a tracking dot does not answer that.

Tempo pairs delivery status with the exact address, the recipient’s details and a confirmation message at handoff. Sign-in and recovery use email or phone, so a customer can get back into an active order without a support call. I wrote those confirmation messages myself, and rewrote them three times until they sounded like a person rather than a system.

columns.title: I shipped the service six weeks before the app
columns.body:
The business needed to take orders while the mobile product was still in progress. So I designed a one-page site that explains Tempo’s promise, gives customers a phone number to request a delivery, and invites couriers and partners to join.

For six weeks the entire product was that page and the founder’s phone. It was humbling, and it was the best research I did: every call was a customer explaining, in their own words, what they wanted from a route. Several of those phrases are now labels in the app.

sections.title: A system the team can extend without me

items.label: Readable type for maps, commerce and account flows
One green that connects the brand, the route line and every confirming action
Spacing rules that hold on dense mobile screens with a map underneath
Inputs, buttons, cards, feedback and states — documented so a new category is data, not design

sections.title: The route is the product, not a final tracking screen
sections.body:
Tempo’s broad catalogue could have produced a collection of unrelated ordering flows. Treating the route as a persistent product layer gave them one structure, and it is the decision the rest of the design hangs on.

It is also the decision I most want to see tested with real money on the table. When a customer adds a third stop, the fee changes and the arrival estimate moves — and I do not yet know whether that reads as the system working or as the price quietly going up. That is a trust question, not a visual one, and no amount of polish settles it.

What I would do differently: test the route sheet in week two, not week six. The wireframe round that failed cost five days; the tab it removed would have cost the product.

sections.title: iCredo
sections.subtitle: A loan you ask for the way you would ask a friend - and understand before you say yes.

sections.title: About the project
sections.body:
iCredo is a mobile lending app for Credo Finance, an Armenian consumer-credit company. Instead of a form, the product opens with a small red robot that asks how much you need, listens to what it is for, and comes back with the offer that fits - then verifies your identity, pays the money out and stays with you as the loan is repaid. Discovery, calculation, KYC, repayment and account status live in one guided flow.

My role. I was the product designer from the first workshop to the component library: product strategy, the conversation model, every core flow, the interface, the design system and the mascot. Copy was written together with the credit team, because the assistant's words are the product.

The constraint I designed around. Consumer credit in Armenia is a last-resort category with an annual rate ceiling of 58%. I could not make the loan cheaper, shorter or less serious. What I could change was whether a person understood what they were agreeing to before they agreed to it.

metadata.label: Services
metadata.value: Product strategy, UX, UI, design system, mascot

metadata.label: Key flow
metadata.value: Ask → understand → offer → verify → receive → manage

sections.title: Nine fields became one question, and nobody had to be brave to ask
sections.body: The web calculator that Credo Finance ran before this project asked for everything at once and answered with a monthly payment. iCredo asks for one thing, explains why, and answers with the best offer and the reason it is the best. The same components carry the person from the first bubble to the last repayment, and the mascot carries the feelings the system would otherwise put into error codes.

items.label: question per bubble. The assistant never asks two things at once - that single rule did more for comprehension than any screen I drew
hand-offs from chat to controls: amount, monthly payment and identity. Precision where precision matters, conversation everywhere else
moods the mascot carries - approved, sorry, confused, under maintenance - so outcomes arrive with a face instead of a status code

sections.title: The financial context made clarity non-negotiable

items.label: of the people I surveyed had never tried to take out a loan online. Most had never been asked to.
resident individual borrowers with active loan balances in Armenia - a mass-market product, not a niche one

sections.title: The scariest conversation in finance
sections.body:
Most of the people this product was for had never borrowed online, and every one of them had a private reason for needing the money. The product still had to collect detailed personal and financial information - regulation does not care how you feel about it.

So the brief was not to make the form shorter. It was to make every question feel deliberate, explainable and polite, and the answer feel like advice, not a verdict. A form has no sequence, no tone and no way to say why. A conversation has all three.
sections.subtitle: Asking for money is the moment people feel most judged. Credo's web calculator answered that moment with nine fields, one button and zero explanation.

sections.title: A conversation when context matters. Controls when precision matters.
sections.body: The assistant asks for one decision at a time. The moment an answer has to be exact - an amount, a monthly payment, a document - the chat hands over to chips and inputs, then takes the thread back. Every screen below is the shipped Armenian interface, rebuilt in code from the design file so you can watch it think. Tiran is the customer in every prototype; Credo is the assistant.

items.caption: Where it started: nine fields and a button
items.text: Credo's web calculator was correct and complete and nobody finished it. It asked for an employer before it asked what you needed the money for. Reconstructed here from memory - there is no design file for the before.

items.caption: One question. Then quiet.
items.text: Credo, the assistant, asks the only thing that matters first: how much. Then it asks how you would rather think about the loan - by monthly payment or by term - as two chips, not a paragraph.

items.caption: It asks how you think, not what it needs
items.text: By monthly payment means you name the amount you can live with each month and the assistant works out the term. The number goes into a real input with quick amounts, because a bubble cannot validate zeros.

items.caption: The loan in five lines, before you sign
items.text: Amount, term, monthly payment, loan type and the real annual rate on one card. Three consents tick, and only then does Apply turn blue. Nothing is hidden in a footnote.

items.caption: It checks, and says that it is checking
items.text: The credit-history check takes a few seconds. The screen says so, shows progress, and keeps the logo in the middle so the wait feels like the product working, not the product freezing.

items.caption: Verification you can watch happen
items.text: Photograph the ID card, see it accepted, watch the security ring move from 1/3 to 2/3. It is not invisible. It is understandable, which in this category is better.

items.caption: The loan stays legible after approval
items.text: My Loans turns the commitment into a workspace: status, remaining balance, progress, next payment and a repayment button on one card - and a plain red line when a payment is late.

sections.title: Why this is not a chatbot bolted onto a bank

items.text:
Conversational interfaces fail when they behave like forms wearing a costume: three questions in one message, a wall of text, a typing indicator that hides a database call. People skim and answer the wrong one.

I wrote a hard rule into the conversation model: one decision per bubble, never a second question before the first is answered. The assistant's copy was cut until every message fit in three lines on a small phone.

items.value: It asks how you think, not what it needs
items.text:
A lender's data model starts with amount and term. A person's starts with 'what can I pay each month'. The old calculator forced the first on everyone.

The second question is a choice of mental model - by monthly payment or by term - and the rest of the conversation follows the one you picked. The maths adapts to the person, not the other way round.

items.value: Numbers live in controls, not bubbles
items.text:
My first prototype let people type an amount into the chat. They typed 100000 when they meant 1,000,000, and the assistant cheerfully priced the wrong loan.

Anything that must be exact is a control: quick-amount chips, a formatted input, a document frame. The chat frames the question; the control takes the answer; the chat confirms it back in a blue bubble.

items.value: The whole loan on one card, before you sign
items.text:
Consumer credit hides its price in schedules and footnotes. People sign a monthly payment and discover the annual rate later, from a relative.

The summary card puts amount, term, monthly payment, loan type and the real annual rate in five lines, and the three legal consents are checkboxes you tick yourself. Apply only turns blue after the third.

items.value: It does not leave after the money arrives
items.text:
Most lending flows end at approval. The relationship ends there too, and every later question becomes a phone call.

The same component system continues into My Loans: balance, progress, next payment, repayment actions and the schedule, in the same language the assistant used on day one - including a plain red line when you are late.

items.value: A face instead of a status code
items.text:
Asking for money is the moment people feel most judged, and a photographed loan officer carries that judgment into the interface. Error states written by the system - 'request failed', 'invalid input' - make it worse at the exact moment trust is thinnest.

The red robot fronts every outcome. It celebrates an approval, apologises for an error, thinks through an unclear answer and wears a hard hat during maintenance, so the product speaks with a face people already smile at.

sections.body: Five product decisions and one character, each with the problem it solves and the screen that solves it.

sections.title: Verification you can watch happen
sections.body:
Identity checks are where people leave. Not because the check is hard, but because they cannot see where they are in it or what happens to the photo they just took.

So the KYC flow shows its work: what is being requested, what has already been completed, and how far the security ring is from full. I did not try to make verification invisible. In a last-resort lending product, invisible reads as suspicious. Understandable reads as safe.

sections.title: My first assistant talked too much. I let it.
sections.body:
I was in love with the idea of a conversation, so the first prototype conversed. It welcomed you. It explained the company. It told you what it was about to ask before it asked it, and then asked it, and then confirmed that it had asked it. Four bubbles before the first question. I showed it to a colleague who reads faster than anyone I know, and I watched her scroll past all of it and tap the input.

The second lesson was worse. When the amount was typed into the chat as free text, a participant wrote a number with the wrong count of zeros, the assistant priced it happily, and she only noticed at the offer screen. She laughed. I did not.

Both fails became the two rules the product still runs on: a bubble is for one question and nothing else, and a number is never a bubble. The welcome speech was cut to five words. The amount got a real input with formatting. The assistant became a lot quieter, and the conversation became a lot better - which is a note I have since applied to myself in meetings.

sections.title: What the first usability sessions were built to break
sections.body:
Can a chat make required questions feel clearer than a form? I watched for whether people understood why the assistant was asking each question, especially at the moment the conversation moved from a casual amount into personal details. The tell was hesitation: a pause before income was the signal that the 'why' sentence was missing or too long.

Can a person enter a number with confidence? The design pairs an open amount input with quick amount choices and repayment modes, so nobody has to invent the interaction model themselves. I counted corrections - every time a participant went back to change the amount was a point against the input.

Can a person understand an active loan at a glance? The post-approval workspace puts status, remaining balance, progress, next payment and repayment actions on one card. The test was a single question: 'when is your next payment and how much?' - answered without scrolling, or not.

These are the hypotheses the prototype was built to test and the design responses to them. The documented session notes are the next thing to add to this page.

sections.title: Why a mascot? A face for the scariest conversation in finance
sections.body:
Asking for money is the moment people feel most judged. A human loan officer - even a photographed, smiling one - carries that judgment into the interface. The mascot removes it: nobody feels evaluated by a small red robot. It turns an interrogation into a guided conversation and gives the assistant a consistent, recognisable presence across the whole product.

The mascot also does functional work. It carries the app's emotional states - celebrating an approval, apologising for an error, thinking through an unclear answer, wearing a hard hat during maintenance - so the product can communicate outcomes with feeling instead of system jargon. In a category where trust is the whole battle, a character users smile at is not decoration. It is the trust mechanism.

For the record, the first version looked like a fire hydrant with anxiety. The construction sketch below is where it started to become someone.

sections.caption: Making of: from construction sketch to finished character.

sections.title: The mark arrives before the first question does.
sections.body: A lending assistant asks people to trust it in the first ten seconds, and the first of those seconds happens on the home screen, next to every other app they already trust. So the mark is built to hold at icon size: four blades 90° apart, every edge landing on one of three circles, nothing fine enough to turn to mush at 60pt.

sections.title: A system for a product that keeps growing

items.label: Conversation patterns for guidance and decision making
items.text:
Grey bubble asks, blue bubble answers - the two colours are the whole grammar.

One question per bubble, three lines at most.

Chips for choices, an input for numbers, the chat confirms both back.

Name labels so a screenshot still reads as a conversation.

items.label: Secure capture with visible progress
items.text:
One document per screen, one sentence of instruction.

A dashed frame shows where the card goes before the camera opens.

The 1/3 → 2/3 → 3/3 ring says how much is left, not just that something is loading.

Confirm stays grey until the capture is accepted.

items.label: Account, repayment, status and schedule patterns
items.text:
One card per loan: name, status pill, remaining balance, progress bar, next payment.

Green means on track, grey means finished, red text means late - no other colours.

The primary action is always the same button in the same place: repay.

Details live one tap deeper, never on the card.

items.label: Complexity kept, made understandable
items.text:
A loan has a dozen numbers; each screen shows the one you decide on now and keeps the rest one tap away.

Labels are plain Armenian, never the credit team's vocabulary.

One blue for actions, one green for progress, one red for the logo and lateness.

8px spacing grid, 12px radii, 15px body - the same rhythm from first bubble to last repayment.

sections.title: Business context
sections.quote: Credo Finance's stated goal is to give consumers a personal approach and flexible, convenient services. The product direction translated that goal into a mobile flow people could understand before they committed.

person.name: Bella Gabrielyan
person.role: Executive Director & Board Member, Credo Finance

sections.annotationText: Leadership context - not a direct testimonial

sections.title: The right interface does not make the decision disappear
sections.body:
Borrowing is personal, consequential and sometimes stressful. I did not try to design that away. I gave people a calmer way to ask, a clearer reason for every question, one honest recommendation instead of a menu, and a place to keep track of what they had agreed to.

If I did it again I would put the 'why' sentences in front of the credit team on day one instead of week three - that is where the real product decisions were hiding. And I would keep the robot. The robot was right.

The strongest next step is to replace the validation hypotheses above with the documented session notes and a proper before-and-after of the calculator.

sections.title: LIGA Mobile
sections.subtitle: The insurance app you hope never to open, redesigned around the ten minutes when you have to. That work exposed a wider gap: the app also had to help people complete a policy sale.

sections.title: About the project
sections.body:
LIGA Mobile is the customer app of Liga Insurance, an Armenian insurer. It holds every policy a household has - compulsory motor liability, casco, travel, property - and it does the two things a policy document cannot: it registers an accident from the side of the road, and it tells you where your claim is without a phone call.

An insurance app is judged on one day, and it is not the day you buy the policy. Nobody opens one for pleasure; every session is an errand or an emergency. The old app was built for the errand.

My role. I led the redesign end to end: the product map, the claim and accident flows, every screen, the component library and the Armenian interface copy. The claim states were written with the settlement team, because the words in that timeline are the product.

The constraint I designed around. Compulsory motor liability is bought by people who did not choose to be customers, and used by people who are having a bad day. I could not make an accident pleasant. What I could change is whether a person standing next to a damaged car knows exactly what to do next, and whether the claim they file comes back approved instead of suspended.

On the numbers above. Those are the product’s reach, not this redesign’s result. What the redesign itself moved is further down, and measured.

sections.title: The claim left the call centre and moved to the side of the road
sections.body: The redesign started with the moment a policy document cannot handle: an accident at the roadside. It became the lens for rebuilding the rest of the app, including the policy journeys that had to work before and after that moment. The evidence comes after the flows it explains.

items.label: Filing a claim
items.before: Call the hotline, wait in a queue, and describe the scene to a stranger who asks the same nine questions every time.
items.after: Four steps answered standing at the car, each one saved the moment it is finished.

items.label: Knowing where the claim is
items.before: Call and ask, and hope the person reading the database field says something you can act on.
items.after: Five states on the claim itself, each with the date it was entered, and a plain sentence whenever an expected date moves.

items.label: No signal at the roadside
items.before: Start again later, if the photographs are still any use by then.
items.after: The report opens offline, keeps the photos on the device, and syncs when the network comes back.

sections.title: The worst ten minutes of your year, on hold
sections.subtitle: A claim used to start with a phone call from the side of a road, and continue with a queue, a reference number by SMS, and two weeks of not knowing.
sections.body:
The old journey was not badly designed. It was not designed at all: an app to view policies, and a hotline for everything that mattered. The moment a person actually needed the insurer, the product handed them over to a queue and a stranger who asked, in order, for the same nine things every time.

Two things went wrong there, and both cost money. People described the accident instead of documenting it, so the file arrived incomplete and the claim was suspended for missing data. And once it was in, nobody could see it, so they phoned to ask - which is how a settlement department ends up spending its day reading statuses aloud.

sections.title: The accident report, taken standing up
sections.body: Four steps, in the order a person can actually answer them, with the camera guided before it opens, every step saved as it is finished, and the whole thing able to start with no signal at all. The screens are rebuilt in code from the design file so they play rather than sit still; the shipped interface is Armenian, and the real exports are further down the page.

items.caption: The two verbs, above everything you own
items.text: The old home screen was a list of policies. This one puts the two things a person actually opens the app to do - register an accident, claim a payout - in a block of their own above the contracts. The paperwork is still there, one scroll down, where paperwork belongs.

items.caption: It has to work where the signal does not
items.text: An accident happens on a road, and roads are where the network is worst. So the report opens offline. The app says so in a sentence rather than a spinner, keeps the photos and the answers on the device, and gives three hours to submit once there is signal again - long enough to drive out of the gap, short enough that the photos still describe the same scene.

items.caption: Photograph the positions, not the dent
items.text: People photograph damage. Assessors need both cars where they stopped, from one position - the shot that proves what happened. So step one asks for one to four photos of the mutual positions and shows an example of exactly that before the camera opens.

items.caption: When and where, without typing
items.text: A date-and-time wheel and a location picker, because a keyboard is the wrong instrument for a wet phone held in one hand. Both fields are required and say so immediately, instead of accepting an empty report politely and failing later.

items.caption: Their document, front and back
items.text: ID card or driving licence, whichever the other driver has on them, photographed both sides, with the document number and a phone number under it. These are the fields whose absence suspends a claim two weeks later, so the app insists on them now, while the other driver is still standing there.

items.caption: Then yours, in the same shape
items.text: Step four is step three again, with your own document. Identical layout on purpose: by now the person knows what the screen wants, and the last step takes a fraction of the time of the first. The button at the bottom is the only one in the flow that does not say Continue.

items.caption: It ends with a sentence, not a number
items.text: The confirmation says what happened and what happens next in one paragraph, and offers the filed report as a document. The claim number is there, but it is not the message - a reference number is not reassurance.

items.caption: A claim that explains itself
items.text: Received, accepted, inspected, decided, paid - each with the date it happened. When the expected date moves, the app says so, with the new date and the reason, which is the single question the hotline used to answer all day.

sections.title: Why this is not a policy PDF with a login
sections.body: Six product decisions, each with the problem it solves and the screen that solves it.

items.text:
Insurance apps are organised around the company: products, policies, documents, profile. That map is correct and useless at the moment a person opens the app with shaking hands.

The home screen is organised around the two things a person actually opens the app to do. Register an accident and claim a payout sit in a block of their own above the contracts; everything the company cares about is one quiet tap deeper.

Most suspended claims are not fraud or disputes. They are photographs of a scratch, taken from six inches away, that prove nothing about who hit whom.

The rule and the example come before the camera: both cars, one position, one to four photos. The step validates that something usable is there rather than accepting an empty report and failing the person a fortnight later.

A roadside is not a place where forms get finished. The police arrive, the cars have to be moved, the other driver wants to talk, the battery is at four per cent.

An unfinished report parks itself on the home screen with the time left to complete it and resumes exactly where it stopped, so an interruption costs nothing and the claim still gets filed.

items.value: A claim with a public status
items.text:
"Where is my money" is the most expensive question in insurance: it is asked by phone, repeatedly, by someone who is already unhappy, and answered by a person reading a database field aloud.

The claim carries its own five-state timeline with dates, and when a date slips it says so in a sentence. The status is the product's answer, not the call centre's.

items.value: A policy that shows its own expiry
items.text:
Cover lapses because an end date lives in an email from last year. Uninsured driving is a fine at best, and at worst it is the accident above with no claim at the end of it.

Every policy carries a bar from start date to expiry, the bar turns red in the list while there is still time to act, and renewal sits on the policy itself rather than in a menu.

Premiums are paid in instalments, and an instalment somebody cannot pay in full quietly becomes a lapsed policy - the worst outcome for both sides.

Payment offers the scheduled instalment or a payment against the principal, with the service fee and the total shown before they commit rather than after.

sections.title: My first version was designed for a calm person
sections.body:
The first accident flow was one tidy screen. Every field visible, nothing hidden, a single confident button at the bottom - the kind of form that wins arguments in a design review because you can see the whole thing at once. At my desk it took about ninety seconds to fill in.

Then I tried to imagine filling it in while standing in the rain, holding the phone in one hand and my own documents in the other, with the other driver explaining loudly whose fault it was. The form was fine. The situation was not. One long screen means one long scroll, one wrong tap loses the lot, and nothing is saved until the end.

Breaking it into four steps made it longer on paper and far shorter in practice, because each step is one question, each step is saved, and the flow can be abandoned and picked up again. The lesson I keep from it: the test for an emergency screen is not how fast it goes when everything is fine.

sections.title: What the prototype was built to break
sections.body:
Can a person file a usable report one-handed, standing up? The test is not time to completion but completeness: does the file that arrives contain the four things an assessor needs, without a follow-up call. I watched for hesitation at the photo step, which is where a person decides whether the app knows what it wants.

Does the interruption really cost nothing? Every session was interrupted on purpose - phone locked, app killed, a call taken mid-step - to see whether the report came back and whether the person believed it had.

Does the status answer the question, or provoke the call? The measure is whether someone reading the timeline can say what happens next and roughly when, in their own words. A status that needs explaining is a status that generates a phone call.

These are the hypotheses the prototype was built to test and the design responses to them. Documented session findings belong here in their place.

sections.title: The quiet half of the product
sections.body: Between accidents, the app is an errand: what do I own, when does it end, what do I owe, what happened to that claim. The same components answer all four.

items.caption: Every policy, with its expiry visible
One policy and the claims attached to it
Claims, each with a status on the card
Pay the instalment, or what you can

sections.title: A system built for one bad day and many dull ones

items.label: Status, timeline and the words in between
items.text:
Five states, one order, never reworded: received, accepted, inspected, decided, paid.

Every state carries the date it happened, not just the fact that it did.

A moved date is always explained in a sentence, never a code.

Status colour is a label, not decoration: blue in progress, green settled, amber delayed.

items.label: Photographs an assessor can actually use
items.text:
Every camera step shows an example before it opens the camera.

The rule is written in the words of the task: both cars, one position.

Documents are always front and back, in that order, in one card.

An empty required step fails at the step, not at submission.

items.label: A policy that keeps its own time
items.text:
One card per policy: class, number, vehicle, dates, progress.

The bar runs start to expiry, so cover is a length and not a date to remember.

Expiring turns red in the list while acting is still possible.

Renewal and termination live on the policy, never in a settings menu.

items.label: Complexity kept, made survivable
items.text:
One red in the whole app, spent on the accident button and destructive confirmations.

Grey carries everything else, so hierarchy is one decision rather than a competition.

Armenian first: every layout is measured with the longest real Armenian label, not the English one.

One step, one question, one thumb - if a screen needs two hands, it is the wrong screen.

sections.title: You cannot design away the accident
sections.body:
Nothing in this app makes a crash less unpleasant. What it can do is remove the second disaster - the one made of missing photographs, suspended files and unanswered phone calls - and that turned out to be almost entirely a design problem rather than an insurance one.

The decision I would defend in any review is making the home screen boring on purpose. Everything grey except one button reads as an under-designed screen for about a second, until you imagine the person it is for.

What I would do differently: get the settlement team into the room in week one rather than week four. Every genuinely good decision in the claim timeline came from someone who had spent a year answering that phone.

sections.title: 8 Images
sections.subtitle: A 3D product configurator that has to work inside someone else's page, at a size you don't control, on a model you didn't choose.

sections.title: About the project
sections.body:
8 Images is a 3D product visualisation tool for furniture merchants. A merchant uploads a model, groups its meshes into named parts, builds materials, attaches them per part, and embeds the result on their own storefront - so a shopper can change the finish and look at the thing from any angle without anyone photographing every combination.

The hard part was never the rendering. It is that everyone in the chain has a different fluency: the merchant who has never opened Blender, the interior designer, and the 3D artist who has. One tool, three levels of comfort with 3D, and a viewer that ends up on a website none of them controls.

My role. Principal product designer, December 2023 to May 2026, working for Ivan Bobrovnikov. I owned design across the model editor, the material system, the embeddable viewer, and the account and workspace surfaces.

sections.title: The viewer had to survive a page I would never see
sections.body: Three constraints shaped every other decision, and not one of them is about rendering. Each is a load the interface had to carry.

items.label: The model
items.before: An arbitrary mesh, exported by someone else, with no names in it.
items.after: Seven named parts on one product, so a shopper has something to point at.

items.label: The library
items.before: 2,189 materials in one catalogue, 2,026 of them textile.
items.after: Thirteen sets, sixteen swatches to a page, 127 options reachable on a single chair seat.

items.label: The embed
items.before: Three fixed sizes, which is not how a merchant's page is shaped.
items.after: Any size the merchant drags to, with the menu, the view strip and the zoom intact.

sections.title: A file the web cannot open
sections.body:
A furniture merchant has two things that do not fit together: a 3D model built for a rendering package, and a product page built for photographs. The model is heavy - the demo firetruck alone is a megabyte of mesh before a single texture loads - and it arrives as an undifferentiated lump of geometry with no idea which triangles are the seat and which are the legs.

Between those two things there was nothing. Not a rendering problem: a naming problem, a reduction problem, and a fitting problem. The rest of this page is those three.

sections.title: I built a 3D editor out of 2D habits
sections.body: Every convention here is borrowed from tools the audience already uses. That was the whole bet, and it is the one I argued hardest for.

items.text:
3D software presents geometry as a scene graph. Graphics tools present it as a stack of layers, and almost everyone in this market has used one of those.

So meshes are layers. Selecting, reordering and renaming work the way they do in an image editor, and the merchant never learns a new mental model to do the one job they came for.

The same borrowing, one level down. A path is a group, because that is the word the audience already has for it.

Consistency here is not tidiness. It is what lets someone who has only ever grouped objects in Figma do the equivalent thing to a mesh without being taught.

Docked panels eat the canvas, and the canvas is the product. So the panels float, the way Figma's do, and the model keeps the room.

It also rehearses the real constraint: if the interface can give up its own space on a desktop, it can survive being squeezed into a merchant's page later.

A shopper cannot choose a material for a mesh. They choose one for the seat, the legs, the top.

So grouping meshes into named parts is not a modelling step, it is the step that makes the product shoppable. Chair back, chair base, chair seat, chair cushions, table top, table legs, vase - seven names, and the configurator writes itself.

sections.title: Maps are a stack, not a form.
sections.body: Switch a map on and the render answers. This is the screen I argued for and won.

sections.title: An arbitrary mesh, and the names that make it shoppable
sections.body:
This is the real thing - toy-firetruck.glb, exactly as the product serves it: Draco-compressed, 1,066 KB, straight out of Blender. The list beside it is not typed into this page. It is read back out of the file at runtime, which is why it says what it says.

Ten named meshes arrived with the model. Click one and the rest fall away. That is the entire argument of the product in one gesture: geometry is not shoppable, but Ladder Turret is.

sections.title: From a lump of geometry to something a shopper can point at
sections.body: Four moves. Each one exists because of the load named above it.

items.caption: Upload the model
items.text: The merchant brings whatever their maker exported. Nothing is renamed, nothing is optimised by hand - the model arrives as it is, and the work of making it legible happens here rather than in a 3D package the merchant does not own.

items.caption: Name the parts
items.text: Meshes are grouped into parts, and the parts get the words a shopper would use. This is the whole trick: after it, every other screen has something to talk about. Seven names on this product is what turns a mesh into a configurator.

items.caption: Attach the materials
items.text: Materials are built in their own editor - imported, or made from layers - and attached per part. One chair seat carries 127 of them, paged sixteen at a time, which is only usable because the library is already cut into thirteen sets.

items.caption: Fit it to a page you will never see
items.text: Desktop, tablet, phone, and a custom size the merchant drags to, with the pixel dimensions live while they drag. The viewer reflows and the chrome stays. This is the step the first version got wrong.

sections.title: I designed for three screen sizes. Merchants have infinite.
sections.body:
The first version of the embed offered desktop, tablet and phone. Three breakpoints, the way a website is built, and it looked correct in every review because reviews happen at the sizes you designed for.

Then it went into a real page. A merchant's product column is not 1440, or 768, or 393. It is whatever is left after their header, their gallery and their sidebar have taken what they need - and at those in-between widths the viewer was wrong in the way only fixed breakpoints can be: a menu that overlapped the model, a thumbnail strip that clipped, controls that had nowhere to go.

The fix was to stop treating size as a set of cases and start treating it as a range. A custom size with a drag handle and a live pixel readout, and chrome that is laid out against the container rather than against a breakpoint. It is the least glamorous decision in the project and the one that made the product embeddable.

sections.title: The viewer, running in this page
sections.body:
This is the shipped product, embedded the same way a merchant embeds it — which makes this portfolio page one of the arbitrary containers the thing was built to survive. Drag the frame and watch the chrome hold.

It loads on sight, and it costs what it costs: 2,273 KB across 65 requests — a megabyte of mesh, a 387 KB lighting environment, and a Draco decoder to unpack the geometry. A page that argues heavy 3D can feel light should be honest about what heavy means.

sections.eyebrow: A small thing that was not small
sections.title: Models became Products, Showrooms became Scenes
sections.body:
The navigation shipped with different words than the ones it was designed with. Research moved them: Models and Showrooms are what the people who build 3D call these things, and they quietly told everyone else that the tool was not for them.

Products and Scenes are what a merchant calls them. Renaming a primary navigation item late is expensive and worth it - it is the cheapest possible way to widen who thinks a tool is meant for them.

sections.title: Scenes is still a waiting room
sections.body:
The third module - putting several products into one room and rendering the set - is designed and not live. Open it in the product today and you get a sentence and a request-early-access link.

That empty state is the part I would defend. A module that does not exist yet still has a state, and the honest one tells you what it will do and offers you a way to be told when it does, rather than hiding the navigation item and pretending the ambition is not there.

sections.title: The 3D was the easy part
sections.body:
Two and a half years on this, and almost none of the work that mattered was about geometry. It was about naming: parts so a shopper can point, sets so a catalogue of two thousand textiles can be chosen from, panels and layers borrowed from tools people already knew so that nobody had to be taught.

The decision I would defend in any review is the boring one - laying the viewer out against its container instead of against three breakpoints. It is invisible when it works, and it is the only reason the thing can live on a page I will never see.
